title: Permanent skilled visas make up a minority of net overseas migration; students and other temporary entrants make up most of it
oneLiner: A cap on total net migration need not touch the skilled program at all.
body: The permanent skilled stream is set each year in the budget and has run at roughly 130,000 to 140,000 places, many granted to people already in the country. Net overseas migration is several times larger and is driven mainly by temporary arrivals. A cap could therefore be met without reducing the skilled intake.
contextBackground: The distinction between the permanent program, which the government sets, and net overseas migration, which it mostly does not, is lost in much public debate. It changes what a cap would actually cut.
contextDisagreement: The composition is not disputed. The argument is whether the skilled program could realistically be held harmless under a cap, given that many skilled visas go to former students.

evidenceItems.citation: Centre for Population, Population Statement — net overseas migration by visa category

otherClaim.title: Employers in health, aged care and construction report persistent shortages that skilled migration helps fill

claimItself.title: Employers in health, aged care and construction report persistent shortages that skilled migration helps fill
claimItself.oneLiner: The government's own shortage list shows the same occupations year after year.
claimItself.body: Jobs and Skills Australia's annual occupation shortage list has consistently included nurses, aged-care workers, electricians, carpenters and other trades. Employers in those sectors argue that skilled and temporary migration is the only way to staff them at current wages and training rates.
